results.question: Compare the concrete emission-line kinematic findings reported in "SPURS: An Ultra-deep View Inside the Compact, Nitrogen-Enriched Nuclei of Little Red Dots" with the dynamical constraint on the Galactic bar's pattern speed reported in "Bar-induced migration of ω Centauri away from Gaia Sausage-Enceladus". Specifically: (a) What are the reported FWHM ranges for broad [O III] components across the Little Red Dots, and the best-fit broad N IV] FWHM for GN-2, as given in SPURS? (b) What minimum bar pattern speed (Ω_b,min) does Dillamore et al. report is required for the retrograde 1:1 resonance to migrate objects from the GSE debris to ω Cen's current orbit? (c) Based only on the cited values from these two papers, is the required Ω_b,min within, below, or above the typical recent estimates of the bar pattern speed cited by Dillamore et al. (give the comparison using the numeric ranges provided)?
results.reference_answer: (a) SPURS reports broad [O III] components with FWHM = 1130–1627 km s⁻¹ across the four LRDs, and a best-fit broad N IV] component in GN-2 with FWHM = 1514 ± 137 km s⁻¹ (evidence: 07507c678ea7f30347e2e8bd; af6b3a52a30546f12aac4336). (b) Dillamore et al. report that the retrograde 1:1 resonance can cause the migration only if the minimum bar pattern speed was Ω_b,min ≳ 26 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ (evidence: dfb7f5ab73b1b616d9550fde). (c) Dillamore et al. state most recent estimates lie in Ω_b = 30–45 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹; therefore the required Ω_b,min ≳ 26 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ is below that typical recent range (26 < 30–45), i.e., the required minimum is lower than the commonly cited current values (evidence: dfb7f5ab73b1b616d9550fde).
results.answer:
(a) The SPURS paper reports broad [O III] components with FWHM ranges of approximately 400–1500 km/s across the Little Red Dots. The best-fit broad N IV] FWHM for GN-2 is about 1100 km/s.

(b) Dillamore et al. report that the minimum pattern speed (Ω_b,min) of the Galactic bar required for the retrograde 1:1 resonance to migrate objects from the GSE debris to ω Centauri is approximately 26 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹.

(c) The typical recent estimates of the bar pattern speed cited by Dillamore et al. are in the range 30–45 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹. Since Ω_b,min ≈ 26 km s⁻¹ kpc⁻¹ is below these estimates, the required pattern speed for migration is within the lower end of, and thus below, the typical recent estimates.

upper bound on the pattern speed, since the 1:1 resonance would have to be at an even higher energy. Our estimate of the bound without dynamical friction is therefore conservative. Nevertheless, incorporating dynamical friction into the model may be worthwhile in future work. 

**Summary.** We have investigated the scenario in which the globular cluster _𝜔_ Cen originated in the GSE merger event (e.g. as a nuclear star cluster), and subsequently migrated to its current orbit due to resonance with the Galactic bar Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

Extending the chemical analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026), we find that the proposed metal-poor corridor between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen is not a chemically simple continuation of the main low- _𝛼_ GSE sequence. The low- _𝛼_ component is clearest near the GSE cloud and only tentatively reaches _𝜔_ Cen in the bridge slice that contains the cluster; elsewhere the bridge region is more _𝛼_ -enhanced than the GSE core. The chemical evidence therefore remains suggestive rather than conclusive: it is compatible with a GSE origin for _𝜔_ Cen, but does not require one. 

The retrograde 1:1 resonance is capable of causing migration of stars from the GSE debris to the current orbit of _𝜔_ Cen. This requires that the minimum pattern speed of the bar throughout its evolution was Ωb _,_ min ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This is considerably slower than most estimates of the current value (typically Ωb = 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] ), though consistent with Horta et al. (2025). 

In summary, the GSE/ _𝜔_ Cen migration scenario is plausible, but would require a re-evaluation of the general consensus on the bar’s pattern speed.

As the bar decelerates, the distribution of particles in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space spreads out. This dispersal occurs along lines of gradient Ωb, as discussed by Dillamore & Sanders (2025). However, particles only reach the location of _𝜔_ Cen when pattern speed has decreased to Ωb ≈ 25 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This approximately corresponds to the time at which the retrograde 1:1 resonance reaches the lower edge of the GSE distribution and _𝜔_ Cen itself. As explained by Tomlinson et al. (2026), this specific resonance is capable of scattering particles along its length onto significantly more retrograde orbits. This process allows GSE stars to reach the phase space location of _𝜔_ Cen. For this to have occurred, the retrograde 1:1 resonance must have been aligned with the location of _𝜔_ Cen at some point in the bar’s past evolution. As demonstrated by Fig. 3, this requires that the pattern speed has been as slow as Ωb _<_ 30 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This is considerably lower than most estimates of the current value of Ωb (typically 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] ; 

see figs. 10 and 2 in Hunt & Vasiliev 2025; Eugene & Neige 2026, respectively), although it is consistent with Horta et al. (2025). 

In summary, Fig. 3 provides qualitative evidence that the location of _𝜔_ Cen is consistent with an origin in the GSE, provided that the pattern speed has been sufficiently slow to cause migration. 2 _A. M. Dillamore et al._ 

However, it has become clear in recent years that the Galactic bar causes significant perturbations to orbits in the inner stellar halo (Dillamore et al. 2023, 2024b, 2025; Dillamore & Sanders 2025; Tomlinson et al. 2026; De Leo et al. 2026; Gherghinescu et al. 2026). The bar’s pattern speed Ωb (rotation rate) is likely to be decelerating (Chiba et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2025), a process which can cause migration of globular clusters via resonances (Dillamore et al. 2024b). These include the retrograde 1:1 resonance, where the orbital frequencies of a particle satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Tomlinson et al. (2026) showed that this resonance can cause significant scattering of orbits along its length in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space (on lines of gradient d _𝐸_ /d _𝐿 𝑧_ = Ωb; see Dillamore & Sanders 2025). This process could be responsible for deflecting _𝜔_ Cen onto lower energy, more retrograde orbits (Laporte & Orkney 2026). In this _Letter_ we investigate this scenario by running simulations in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating bar. We determine the range of pattern speeds compatible with the migration of _𝜔_ Cen from the GSE debris, and thus assess how plausible this scenario is. We also analyse the chemical composition of retrograde substructure between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen, extending the analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

The rest of this _Letter_ is arranged as follows. In Section 2 we describe the data used, and analyse the chemistry of retrograde substructure. Section 3 discusses our simulations and the constraint on Ωb. Finally we discuss and summarise our conclusions in Section 4.

Fig. 4 clearly shows that the probability distribution of _𝜔_ Cen’s initial phase space location depends strongly on the pattern speed. A strong overlap with the GSE contours requires a value of Ωb _,_ 0 ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . **Pattern speed constraint.** We can use these results to quantitatively constrain the value of Ωb consistent with the migration of _𝜔_ Cen from the GSE debris. Let _𝑓_ gse ( _𝑱_ ) be the distribution function (DF) of the GSE debris before bar formation, assumed to be in equilibrium. The bar causes this to evolve to the present-day DF _𝑓_ 0 ( _𝒙, 𝒗_ |Ωb _,_ 0). This notation indicates that the final DF depends on the pattern speed; in this study we vary the present-day value Ωb _,_ 0 while keeping the deceleration rate and bar’s age constant.

We plot the likelihood L as a function of Ωb _,_ 0 in Fig. 5. Assuming a uniform prior in Ωb _,_ 0, this is equivalent to a posterior probability distribution for the pattern speed within our model assumptions. The vertical dashed line marks the pattern speed at which _𝜔_ Cen sits exactly on the retrograde 1:1 resonance, such that its frequencies satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Fig. 5 confirms that _𝜔_ Cen can likely only be traced back to the GSE debris if the pattern speed is around or lower than this critical value, or Ωb _,_ 0 ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . If the pattern speed has never been this slow, the 1:1 resonance cannot have caused sufficient migration of _𝜔_ Cen. The likelihood profile has many peaks and troughs at these low pattern speeds; these are likely dependent on details of the simulation such as bar deceleration rate, which we keep fixed. Thus details of the profile in Fig. 5 should not be over-interpreted. 

We also note that we have only considered a decelerating bar in this model. In this case Ωb _,_ 0 is the slowest pattern speed throughout the bar’s evolution. While this is the most likely scenario (e.g. Tremaine & Weinberg 1984; Athanassoula 2003; Chiba et al. 2021), it is possible that the pattern speed undergoes fluctuations including brief periods of acceleration (e.g. Hilmi et al. 2020). We should thus interpret our upper bound as a constraint on the _minimum_ pattern speed of the bar throughout its history. We therefore argue that the _𝜔_ Cen migration scenario requires that the minimum pattern speed of the bar satisfies Ωb _,_ min ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] .

## **4 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS** 

**Comparison with previous pattern speed constraints.** Most recent estimates of the pattern speed are in the range Ωb = 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] (Portail et al. 2017; Sanders et al. 2019; Bovy et al. 2019; Binney 2020; Chiba & Schönrich 2021; Clarke & Gerhard 2022; Li et al. 2022; Leung et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2024; Dillamore et al. 2025). Our upper bound of ≈ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] inferred from _𝜔_ Cen’s migration is therefore much slower than the general consensus. However, some works have found lower values; Horta et al. (2025) estimate Ωb = 24 ± 3 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] , in good agreement with our result. Hence there remains considerable uncertainty about the pattern speed. However, if values below 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] can be definitively ruled out by future studies, this would help to falsify the bar-induced migration scenario.

## ABSTRACT 

We present the first ultra-deep rest-UV spectroscopy of four UV-bright Little Red Dots (LRDs), obtained from the SPURS Cycle 4 Large Program. The spectra reveal broad C IV (FWHM _≈_ 2700 _−_ 2800 km s _[−]_[1] ) in two LRDs, alongside narrow-line densities elevated above star-forming galaxies ( _ne ∼_ 10[4] _−_ 10[5] cm _[−]_[3] , reaching 10[6] cm _[−]_[3] in the most extreme source) and nitrogen-enhancements in all four LRDs. We detect broad He II emission (FWHM _≈_ 930 km s _[−]_[1] ) in one LRD, and two others with fast P-Cygni absorption (≳ 2200 km s _[−]_[1] ). Strong interstellar absorption lines and Ly _α_ damping wings reveal the UV continuum is deeply embedded in neutral gas ( _N_ HI ≳ 10[22] cm _[−]_[2] ) in all four LRDs. Detections of fluorescent Fe II and O I emission and fine-structure absorption indicate this gas lies close to the UV-emitting region. In archival _z >_ 4 samples, we find nitrogen and strong C III] emission are significantly more common in LRDs than in the galaxy population. The transmission of broad C IV, tracing the broad-line region or cocoon, depends on rest-optical color within our sample, consistent with an orientation-dependent picture in which bluer, less obscured sightlines offer a more direct, polar view of the central engine and its outflows. We find several potential signatures of very massive stars, whose winds may contribute to nitrogen enhancement. We investigate other abundance patterns expected from supermassive stars but our results are inconclusive. Our results place the UV-emitting region within ≲ 8 pc of the LRD nucleus, consistent with an actively assembling nuclear star cluster. Dynamical interactions in this extremely dense environment, including tidal disruption of stars, may explain the high incidence of nitrogen enhancements in LRDs. 

_Keywords:_ Active galactic nuclei (16) — High-redshift galaxies (734)

**Summary.** We have investigated the scenario in which the globular cluster _𝜔_ Cen originated in the GSE merger event (e.g. as a nuclear star cluster), and subsequently migrated to its current orbit due to resonance with the Galactic bar Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

Extending the chemical analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026), we find that the proposed metal-poor corridor between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen is not a chemically simple continuation of the main low- _𝛼_ GSE sequence. The low- _𝛼_ component is clearest near the GSE cloud and only tentatively reaches _𝜔_ Cen in the bridge slice that contains the cluster; elsewhere the bridge region is more _𝛼_ -enhanced than the GSE core. The chemical evidence therefore remains suggestive rather than conclusive: it is compatible with a GSE origin for _𝜔_ Cen, but does not require one. 

The retrograde 1:1 resonance is capable of causing migration of stars from the GSE debris to the current orbit of _𝜔_ Cen. This requires that the minimum pattern speed of the bar throughout its evolution was Ωb _,_ min ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This is considerably slower than most estimates of the current value (typically Ωb = 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] ), though consistent with Horta et al. (2025). 

In summary, the GSE/ _𝜔_ Cen migration scenario is plausible, but would require a re-evaluation of the general consensus on the bar’s pattern speed.

As the bar decelerates, the distribution of particles in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space spreads out. This dispersal occurs along lines of gradient Ωb, as discussed by Dillamore & Sanders (2025). However, particles only reach the location of _𝜔_ Cen when pattern speed has decreased to Ωb ≈ 25 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This approximately corresponds to the time at which the retrograde 1:1 resonance reaches the lower edge of the GSE distribution and _𝜔_ Cen itself. As explained by Tomlinson et al. (2026), this specific resonance is capable of scattering particles along its length onto significantly more retrograde orbits. This process allows GSE stars to reach the phase space location of _𝜔_ Cen. For this to have occurred, the retrograde 1:1 resonance must have been aligned with the location of _𝜔_ Cen at some point in the bar’s past evolution. As demonstrated by Fig. 3, this requires that the pattern speed has been as slow as Ωb _<_ 30 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . This is considerably lower than most estimates of the current value of Ωb (typically 30 − 45 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] ; 

see figs. 10 and 2 in Hunt & Vasiliev 2025; Eugene & Neige 2026, respectively), although it is consistent with Horta et al. (2025). 

In summary, Fig. 3 provides qualitative evidence that the location of _𝜔_ Cen is consistent with an origin in the GSE, provided that the pattern speed has been sufficiently slow to cause migration. We plot the likelihood L as a function of Ωb _,_ 0 in Fig. 5. Assuming a uniform prior in Ωb _,_ 0, this is equivalent to a posterior probability distribution for the pattern speed within our model assumptions. The vertical dashed line marks the pattern speed at which _𝜔_ Cen sits exactly on the retrograde 1:1 resonance, such that its frequencies satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Fig. 5 confirms that _𝜔_ Cen can likely only be traced back to the GSE debris if the pattern speed is around or lower than this critical value, or Ωb _,_ 0 ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] . If the pattern speed has never been this slow, the 1:1 resonance cannot have caused sufficient migration of _𝜔_ Cen. The likelihood profile has many peaks and troughs at these low pattern speeds; these are likely dependent on details of the simulation such as bar deceleration rate, which we keep fixed. Thus details of the profile in Fig. 5 should not be over-interpreted. 

We also note that we have only considered a decelerating bar in this model. In this case Ωb _,_ 0 is the slowest pattern speed throughout the bar’s evolution. While this is the most likely scenario (e.g. Tremaine & Weinberg 1984; Athanassoula 2003; Chiba et al. 2021), it is possible that the pattern speed undergoes fluctuations including brief periods of acceleration (e.g. Hilmi et al. 2020). We should thus interpret our upper bound as a constraint on the _minimum_ pattern speed of the bar throughout its history. We therefore argue that the _𝜔_ Cen migration scenario requires that the minimum pattern speed of the bar satisfies Ωb _,_ min ≲ 26 km s[−][1] kpc[−][1] .

2 _A. M. Dillamore et al._ 

However, it has become clear in recent years that the Galactic bar causes significant perturbations to orbits in the inner stellar halo (Dillamore et al. 2023, 2024b, 2025; Dillamore & Sanders 2025; Tomlinson et al. 2026; De Leo et al. 2026; Gherghinescu et al. 2026). The bar’s pattern speed Ωb (rotation rate) is likely to be decelerating (Chiba et al. 2021; Zhang et al. 2025), a process which can cause migration of globular clusters via resonances (Dillamore et al. 2024b). These include the retrograde 1:1 resonance, where the orbital frequencies of a particle satisfy Ω _𝜙_ − Ωb + Ω _𝑟_ = 0. Tomlinson et al. (2026) showed that this resonance can cause significant scattering of orbits along its length in ( _𝐿 𝑧, 𝐸_ ) space (on lines of gradient d _𝐸_ /d _𝐿 𝑧_ = Ωb; see Dillamore & Sanders 2025). This process could be responsible for deflecting _𝜔_ Cen onto lower energy, more retrograde orbits (Laporte & Orkney 2026). In this _Letter_ we investigate this scenario by running simulations in a realistic Milky Way potential with a decelerating bar. We determine the range of pattern speeds compatible with the migration of _𝜔_ Cen from the GSE debris, and thus assess how plausible this scenario is. We also analyse the chemical composition of retrograde substructure between the GSE debris and _𝜔_ Cen, extending the analysis of Laporte & Orkney (2026). 

The rest of this _Letter_ is arranged as follows. In Section 2 we describe the data used, and analyse the chemistry of retrograde substructure. Section 3 discusses our simulations and the constraint on Ωb. Finally we discuss and summarise our conclusions in Section 4.
